newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets find feet after sharp selloff.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets find feet after sharp selloff.

text.p: U.S. financial markets found their feet on Tuesday after a violent reaction to remarks from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto exposed Wall Street's vulnerability to economic and political shocks.
Stocks, bonds and the dollar were firm in morning trading after investors were soothed by Japan's efforts at damage control following market-rattling remarks from Hashimoto.
But Monday's selloff could be an indication of further volatility ahead, particularily in the high-flying stock market, analysts said.
"We're trading at a rich valuation that doesn't give you much of a cushion should some kind of unexpected negative event hit," said Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at JP Morgan.
U.S. markets tumbled on Monday after Hashimoto's comments in New York on the need for foreign exchange stability were taken as a veiled threat by Japan to sell off its U.S. Treasury holdings.
Stocks bore the brunt of the blow, with the Dow tumbling 192.25 points, the second-largest point loss in the history of the average.

But Japanese officials quickly backpeddled from the remarks, with the country's finance minister saying Hashimoto's real intention was not correctly reported, and that Japan had no intention of selling U.S. Treasuries.

The Dow opened sharply higher Tuesday, shooting up more than 80 points in the first half hour of trading. The gains were later trimmed and the blue chip index was up about 47 points at 7651 in midday trading.
"The market was in a position to bounce back and the bounce should stick," said Dan Ascani, president and director of research at Global Market Strategists Inc.
The 30-year Treasury bond was up 5/32, its yield at 6.69 percent from Monday's close at 6.71 percent.
The dollar also firmed against the yen at 114.76/81 yen, up from Monday's close at 114.71/76. The dollar had dipped to 114.10 yen overnight.
"We recovered pretty smartly," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd. "Hashimoto's backpedalling and the Japanese are saying all the right things."
Meanwhile, gold, which initially rallied on Hashimoto's remarks, pulled back. August gold was off 0.70 cents at $340.40 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.
Market players said they did not think Hashimoto's remarks reflected any strategic shift in thinking by the Japanese.
Abby Joseph Cohen, co-chair investment policy committee at Goldman Sachs and Co, said she did not expect a significant change in Japanese participation in U.S. financial markets.
In a research note, Cohen said investors based in Japan were net sellers of $2.3 billion of U.S. equities in 1997's first quarter.

Meanwhile, U.S.-based investors made net purchases of $1.9 billion of Japanese equities in the first quarter, she said. "Review of the actual (Hashimoto) comments, and the relevant flow of funds data, suggest an overreaction by investors," Cohen said in the report.

Hashimoto's remarks followed a sharp two-month runup in stocks that market players said has left the stock market overextended and prone to sharp reactions to disappointing news. "At these levels there's not a whole lot of margin for error," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates.
The Dow had risen more than 1,400 points, or 22 percent, from its 1997 closing low on April 11 through its record closing on Friday at 7796.51.

Stocks could further recover this week if there are no fresh surprises, particularly from economic indicators such as Wednesday's report on durable goods orders, analysts said. They noted buying that typicially comes from portfolio managers at the end of a quarter.
"It's hard to do major damage to the marketplace without significant pieces of news on the economy, especially going into the end of the quarter," White said.
